captions.instagram:
How does an MRI machine work?

A magnet 30,000 times stronger than Earth's, a radio that listens to the hydrogen in your body, and a Fourier transform that turns echoes into a picture. Take an MRI scanner apart in 3D and make T1 and T2 contrast yourself.

→ An MRI scanner is a giant magnet, 30,000 times stronger than Earth’s, that never switches off.
→ Inside: superconducting coils in liquid helium at −269 °C, then gradient coils and a radio antenna.
→ Every hydrogen nucleus in your body is a tiny spinning magnet.
→ In the scanner a few per million line up, and all of them wobble at 64 million times a second.
→ A radio pulse tips the spins over. They fan out and fade, then an echo brings them back.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/mriclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does an MRI machine work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A magnet 30,000 times stronger than Earth's, a radio that listens to the hydrogen in your body, and a Fourier transform that turns echoes into a picture. Take an MRI scanner apart in 3D and make T1 and T2 contrast yourself.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/mriclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/mriclear

In this video:
• A giant magnet that never switches off. An MRI scanner is a superconducting magnet: coils of niobium-titanium wire bathed in liquid helium at about −269 °C, carrying current with no resistance.
• Your hydrogen nuclei are tiny magnets. Each hydrogen nucleus is a spinning proton that acts like a bar magnet.
• A radio pulse, then an echo. A burst of radio waves at exactly that frequency tips the spins sideways, and as they spin they broadcast a faint radio signal.
• Tilting the field to find position. Gradient coils make the field slightly stronger on one side, so each position sings at its own frequency.
• No X-rays, but the magnet is always on. MRI uses no ionising radiation.
• It can watch the brain work. fMRI detects the extra oxygen-rich blood that flows to busy brain areas, diffusion MRI follows water along nerve fibres, and angiography lights up flowing blood.
